notes.summary: Algebra in SSC CGL is mostly about identities: squares, cubes, the x + 1/x family and conditions like a + b + c = 0. Expect 2 to 4 questions in Tier 1 and a few more in Tier 2, with the odd question on linear equations, polynomials, quadratics or the least value of an expression. Learn the identities in these notes and most questions take under a minute.

concepts.title: Start here: what an identity is
concepts.body:
An identity is an equation that is true for every value of the letters, like (a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2. SSC algebra questions are mostly about choosing the right identity, so the work is spotting the link between what is given and what is asked.

Three habits help a beginner:

  • Write what is given and what is asked side by side, then look for an identity that contains both.
  • Check an identity with small numbers. With a = 2, b = 1: (2 + 1)2 = 9 and 4 + 4 + 1 = 9, so it works.
  • When options are numbers, you can often put easy values (a = 1, b = 0 and so on) that satisfy the condition and test the options.

Index rules you will need: xm × xn = xm+n, xm ÷ xn = xm−n, (xm)n = xmn, x0 = 1, x−n = 1/xn.

concepts.title: Square identities
concepts.body:
IdentityUse it when
(a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2you know a + b and ab
(a − b)2 = a2 − 2ab + b2you know a − b and ab
a2 − b2 = (a + b)(a − b)a difference of squares appears
a2 + b2 = (a + b)2 − 2ab = (a − b)2 + 2abthe sum of squares is asked
(a + b)2 − (a − b)2 = 4abyou need ab from a + b and a − b
(a + b)2 + (a − b)2 = 2(a2 + b2)both brackets appear together
a4 + b4 = (a2 + b2)2 − 2a2b2fourth powers are asked
a4 + a2b2 + b4 = (a2 + ab + b2)(a2 − ab + b2)this three-term form appears

Mini example: a + b = 5 and ab = 6. Then a2 + b2 = 25 − 12 = 13, and a4 + b4 = 132 − 2 × 36 = 97. (Check: a = 2, b = 3 gives 16 + 81 = 97.)

Mental arithmetic with the same identities: 1032 = (100 + 3)2 = 10609, and 47 × 53 = 502 − 32 = 2491.

concepts.title: Three-term squares
concepts.body:
(a + b + c)2 = a2 + b2 + c2 + 2(ab + bc + ca).

So if you know any two of these three quantities, you get the third:

  • a + b + c
  • ab + bc + ca
  • a2 + b2 + c2

Mini example: a + b + c = 10 and ab + bc + ca = 31. Then a2 + b2 + c2 = 100 − 62 = 38.

Signs follow the letters: (a − b + c)2 = a2 + b2 + c2 − 2ab − 2bc + 2ca.

concepts.title: Cube identities for two variables
concepts.body:
IdentityShort form
(a + b)3 = a3 + b3 + 3ab(a + b)a3 + b3 = (a + b)3 − 3ab(a + b)
(a − b)3 = a3 − b3 − 3ab(a − b)a3 − b3 = (a − b)3 + 3ab(a − b)
a3 + b3 = (a + b)(a2 − ab + b2)sum of cubes factorised
a3 − b3 = (a − b)(a2 + ab + b2)difference of cubes factorised

Mini example: a + b = 5, ab = 6 gives a3 + b3 = 125 − 90 = 35. (Check: 8 + 27 = 35.)

Division questions use the factorised forms: (8x3 + 27y3) ÷ (2x + 3y). Here a = 2x and b = 3y, so the answer is a2 − ab + b2 = 4x2 − 6xy + 9y2.

concepts.title: The three-variable cube identity
concepts.body:
a3 + b3 + c3 − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a2 + b2 + c2 − ab − bc − ca)

Another form that is handy when the numbers are close together:

a3 + b3 + c3 − 3abc = ½(a + b + c)[(a − b)2 + (b − c)2 + (c − a)2]

Method when a + b + c and ab + bc + ca are given:

  1. Find a2 + b2 + c2 = (a + b + c)2 − 2(ab + bc + ca).
  2. Subtract ab + bc + ca.
  3. Multiply by a + b + c.

Mini example: a = 101, b = 102, c = 103. The sum is 306 and the squared differences are 1 + 1 + 4 = 6, so a3 + b3 + c3 − 3abc = ½ × 306 × 6 = 918.

concepts.title: Conditional identities
concepts.body:
These are facts that hold only when a condition is true. SSC uses them a lot.

IfThen
a + b + c = 0a3 + b3 + c3 = 3abc
a + b + c = 0a2 + b2 + c2 = −2(ab + bc + ca)
a + b + c = 0a2 − bc = b2 − ca = c2 − ab (all equal), and (a + b)(b + c)(c + a) = −abc
a3 + b3 + c3 = 3abceither a + b + c = 0 or a = b = c
a2 + b2 + c2 = ab + bc + caa = b = c
a2 + b2 + c2 = 0 (real numbers)a = b = c = 0

Sum of squares equal to zero. If x2 + y2 − 4x + 6y + 13 = 0, complete the squares: (x − 2)2 + (y + 3)2 = 0. Squares are never negative, so x = 2 and y = −3.

Hidden form. (3x − 1)3 + (4x − 3)3 + (2x + 1)3 = 3(3x − 1)(4x − 3)(2x + 1) means the three brackets add to zero (or are equal). Their sum is 9x − 3 = 0, so x = 1/3. If x = 1/3 is ruled out, the brackets must be equal instead.

Quick check. For a + b + c = 0 questions, try a = 1, b = 1, c = −2 and test the options.

concepts.title: The x + 1/x family
concepts.body:
If x + 1/x = k, square and cube both sides:

  • x2 + 1/x2 = k2 − 2
  • x3 + 1/x3 = k3 − 3k
  • x4 + 1/x4 = (k2 − 2)2 − 2
  • x5 + 1/x5 = (x2 + 1/x2)(x3 + 1/x3) − (x + 1/x)
x + 1/xx2 + 1/x2x3 + 1/x3x4 + 1/x4
371847
41452194
523110527
6341981154

If x − 1/x = k: x2 + 1/x2 = k2 + 2 and x3 − 1/x3 = k3 + 3k. Also (x + 1/x)2 − (x − 1/x)2 = 4.

Special values.

  • x + 1/x = 2 means x = 1, so any power sum xn + 1/xn = 2.
  • x + 1/x = −2 means x = −1.
  • x + 1/x = 1 means x3 = −1, so x3 + 1/x3 = −2.
  • x + 1/x = √3 means x3 + 1/x3 = 3√3 − 3√3 = 0, so x6 = −1.

Hidden form. x2 − 5x + 1 = 0: divide by x to get x + 1/x = 5. For 2x + 1/(2x) style terms, put y = 2x first. For x2 + 1/x2 = 7, x + 1/x = 3 (when x is positive).

concepts.title: Surds and rationalising
concepts.body:
To remove a root from the bottom, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate: 1/(√5 + √3) = (√5 − √3)/(5 − 3) = (√5 − √3)/2.

Pairs that multiply to 1. If a2 − b = 1, then (a + √b)(a − √b) = 1, so 1/(a + √b) = a − √b.

  • x = 2 + √3 gives 1/x = 2 − √3, so x + 1/x = 4 and x2 + 1/x2 = 14.
  • x = 3 + 2√2 gives 1/x = 3 − 2√2, so x + 1/x = 6.
  • x = √2 + 1 gives 1/x = √2 − 1, so x − 1/x = 2.

Square roots of surds. 3 + 2√2 = (√2 + 1)2, so √(3 + 2√2) = √2 + 1. In general a + 2√b = (√m + √n)2 when m + n = a and mn = b.

concepts.title: Simplifying and factorising
concepts.body:
Telescoping products. Multiply by the missing bracket and use a2 − b2 again and again:

(1 − x)(1 + x)(1 + x2)(1 + x4)(1 + x8) = (1 − x2)(1 + x2)(1 + x4)(1 + x8) = … = 1 − x16.

Difference of squares on long brackets. (a + b − c + d)2 − (a − b + c − d)2: the sum of the brackets is 2a and the difference is 2(b − c + d), so the answer is 4a(b − c + d).

Splitting the middle term. For x2 + 7x + 12, find two numbers with product 12 and sum 7 (3 and 4), so x2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4). For 6x2 + 13x + 7, product 6 × 7 = 42 and sum 13 gives 6 and 7, so 6x2 + 6x + 7x + 7 = (6x + 7)(x + 1).

Putting values. To find the value of an expression at given numbers, substitute carefully with brackets, especially for negative numbers: at x = −4, x3 = −64 and x2 = 16.

concepts.title: Polynomials: remainder and factor theorems
concepts.body:
A polynomial is a sum of terms like 3x2 − 5x + 2. Its degree is the highest power. A zero (or root) is a value of x that makes it 0.

  • Division rule: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, and the remainder has a smaller degree than the divisor.
  • Remainder theorem: when p(x) is divided by (x − a), the remainder is p(a). For (2x + 1), use x = −1/2.
  • Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor of p(x) exactly when p(a) = 0.

Mini example: is (x − 1) a factor of x3 − 4x2 + 5x − 2? p(1) = 1 − 4 + 5 − 2 = 0, so yes.

Zeroes of a cubic ax3 + bx2 + cx + d with zeroes α, β, γ:

  • α + β + γ = −b/a
  • αβ + βγ + γα = c/a
  • αβγ = −d/a

So for a3 − 4a2 + 5a − 2 = 0 the roots add to 4.

concepts.title: Quadratic equations
concepts.body:
A quadratic is ax2 + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0. Solve it by factorising or by the formula x = [−b ± √(b2 − 4ac)] / 2a.

Discriminant D = b2 − 4acRoots
D > 0two different real roots
D = 0two equal real roots, each −b/2a
D < 0no real roots

For roots α and β: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. From these:

  • α2 + β2 = (α + β)2 − 2αβ
  • (α − β)2 = (α + β)2 − 4αβ
  • 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/αβ
  • α3 + β3 = (α + β)3 − 3αβ(α + β)

Forming an equation. If the roots are p and q, the equation is x2 − (p + q)x + pq = 0. Mini example: roots 2 and 3 give x2 − 5x + 6 = 0.

concepts.title: Linear equations and word problems
concepts.body:
For two unknowns you need two equations. Solve by elimination (make one coefficient equal, then add or subtract) or by substitution.

Mini example: 2 pencils + 3 pens = ₹55 and 7 pencils + 2 pens = ₹65. Multiply the first by 2 and the second by 3: 4p + 6q = 110 and 21p + 6q = 195. Subtract: 17p = 85, so a pencil costs ₹5 and a pen costs ₹15.

Look for a shortcut first. If 32 pens and 12 pencils cost ₹790, then 8 pens and 3 pencils (exactly one quarter) cost 790 ÷ 4 = ₹197.50. No need to find each price.

Heads and legs. If all animals had 2 legs there would be 2 × heads legs. Each 4-legged animal adds 2 more. So 4-legged animals = (legs − 2 × heads) ÷ 2.

Symmetric systems. If x + y = 8, y + z = 13 and z + x = 17, add all three: 2(x + y + z) = 38, so x + y + z = 19. Then z = 19 − 8 = 11, x = 6, y = 2.

concepts.title: When does a pair of equations have a solution?
concepts.body:
For a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0, compare the ratios of the coefficients.

ConditionSolutionsLines
a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2exactly onecross at one point
a1/a2 = b1/b2 ≠ c1/c2noneparallel
a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2infinitely manythe same line

Mini example: 17x + my + 102 = 0 and 23x + 299y + 138 = 0. For infinitely many solutions, 17/23 = m/299 = 102/138. Since 102/138 = 17/23, m = 299 × 17/23 = 221.

concepts.title: Maximum and minimum values
concepts.body:
Complete the square. ax2 + bx + c with a > 0 has its least value at x = −b/2a, and that value is c − b2/4a. Mini example: x2 − 6x + 14 = (x − 3)2 + 5, so the least value is 5. If a < 0, the same point gives the greatest value.

AM ≥ GM. For positive numbers, the average is at least the geometric mean, with equality when all are equal.

  • x + 1/x ≥ 2 for x > 0 (least value 2 at x = 1).
  • ax + b/x ≥ 2√(ab) for x > 0.
  • If x + y = constant, xy is greatest when x = y.
  • If x + y + z = 1 (all positive), 1/x + 1/y + 1/z is least when x = y = z = 1/3, giving 9.

A square is never negative, so (anything)2 + 5 is at least 5.

varieties.name: Square identities
varieties.how: Write what is given (a + b, a − b, ab) and pick the square identity that contains both the given and the asked parts.

example.q: If a − b = 4 and ab = 21, find a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup>.

varieties.name: Cube identities (two variables)
varieties.how: Use a<sup>3</sup> ± b<sup>3</sup> = (a ± b)<sup>3</sup> ∓ 3ab(a ± b). For division questions, use the factorised forms.

example.q: If a − b = 3 and ab = 10, find a<sup>3</sup> − b<sup>3</sup>.

varieties.name: x + 1/x type
varieties.how: Turn the given into x + 1/x = k (divide a quadratic by x, or add a surd to its reciprocal), then square or cube.

steps: Divide by x: x − 5 + 1/x = 0, so x + 1/x = 5

varieties.name: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc
varieties.how: Find a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup> from (a + b + c)<sup>2</sup>, subtract ab + bc + ca, then multiply by a + b + c.

example.q: If a + b + c = 13 and ab + bc + ca = 54, find a<sup>3</sup> + b<sup>3</sup> + c<sup>3</sup> − 3abc.

varieties.name: Conditional identities
varieties.how: Use the condition to replace one variable, or test easy values that satisfy it (for a + b + c = 0, try 1, 1, −2).

example.q: If x + y + z = 0, find (x<sup>2</sup> + y<sup>2</sup> + z<sup>2</sup>) ÷ (z<sup>2</sup> − xy).
steps: z = −(x + y), so z<sup>2</sup> − xy = x<sup>2</sup> + xy + y<sup>2</sup>

varieties.name: Simplify and evaluate
varieties.how: Look for a hidden identity (difference of squares, telescoping product) before multiplying out. When values are given, substitute with brackets.

example.q: Simplify (1 + x)(1 + x<sup>2</sup>)(1 + x<sup>4</sup>)(1 + x<sup>8</sup>)(1 − x).

varieties.name: Polynomials and remainders
varieties.how: For a remainder on division by (x − a), put x = a. For a factor, set that value to 0. For division by a ± b forms, use the sum or difference of cubes.

example.q: Find the remainder when x<sup>3</sup> − 2x<sup>2</sup> + 4x + 5 is divided by (x − 2).

varieties.name: Quadratic equations and roots
varieties.how: Write α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a, rewrite what is asked in terms of these two, then form x<sup>2</sup> − (sum)x + product = 0 if a new equation is needed.

example.q: If α and β are the roots of 6x<sup>2</sup> + 13x + 7 = 0, find the equation whose roots are α<sup>2</sup> and β<sup>2</sup>.
steps: Check: the roots are −1 and −7/6, whose squares 1 and 49/36 fit

varieties.name: Linear equations and word problems
varieties.how: Name the unknowns, write one equation per fact, then eliminate. Check whether the asked combination is a simple multiple of a given equation.

example.q: Rewa has hens and goats. There are 100 heads and 348 feet. How many goats are there?
steps: Extra feet = 348 − 200 = 148, and each goat adds 2

varieties.name: Unique, none or infinite solutions
varieties.how: Compare a<sub>1</sub>/a<sub>2</sub>, b<sub>1</sub>/b<sub>2</sub> and c<sub>1</sub>/c<sub>2</sub>. No solution: first two equal, third different. Infinite: all three equal.

example.q: For what value of k do 3x − ky + 8 = 0 and 9x − 18y + 20 = 0 have no solution?
steps: Check 1/3 ≠ 2/5, so the lines are parallel

varieties.name: Maximum and minimum values
varieties.how: Complete the square for a quadratic, or use AM ≥ GM for sums of positive terms. The extreme value comes when the square is 0 or the terms are equal.

example.q: Find the least value of x<sup>2</sup> − 6x + 14.
steps: The square is at least 0, and equals 0 at x = 3

tips: Before expanding anything, ask which identity links the given to the asked. Expanding is the slow way.
Put easy values that satisfy the condition (a = 1, b = 1, c = −2 for a + b + c = 0; x = 1 for x + 1/x = 2) and test the options.
A quadratic like x<sup>2</sup> − kx + 1 = 0 is really x + 1/x = k. Divide by x.
Learn the x + 1/x table for k = 3, 4, 5, 6. Those values come up again and again.
If a<sup>2</sup> − b = 1, then a + √b and a − √b are reciprocals of each other.
In word problems, check whether the asked combination is a simple fraction of a given equation before solving fully.
For three variables, the trio a + b + c, ab + bc + ca and a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup> + c<sup>2</sup> go together: any two give the third.
traps: x<sup>3</sup> + 1/x<sup>3</sup> = k<sup>3</sup> − 3k, not k<sup>3</sup> − 3. And x<sup>2</sup> + 1/x<sup>2</sup> from x − 1/x is k<sup>2</sup> + 2, not k<sup>2</sup> − 2.
(a + b)<sup>2</sup> is not a<sup>2</sup> + b<sup>2</sup>, and (a + b)<sup>3</sup> is not a<sup>3</sup> + b<sup>3</sup>.
a<sup>3</sup> + b<sup>3</sup> + c<sup>3</sup> = 3abc does not always mean a + b + c = 0; it can also mean a = b = c.
From (a − b)<sup>2</sup> = 1 you get a − b = ±1. Check the sign the question needs.
For the remainder on dividing by (2x − 1), put x = 1/2, not x = 1 or x = 2.
Watch the signs when substituting negative values: (−4)<sup>3</sup> = −64 but (−4)<sup>2</sup> = 16.
